claim: A voltage divider scales a battery voltage down into an ADC's range: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
draft: The M5StickC Plus2 already has a 2:1 divider on GPIO38 for its own battery. A 2S pack (8.4 V) needs about 3:1 or more to stay under 3.3 V.

claim: A voltage divider scales a battery voltage down into an ADC's range: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
draft: Low-value dividers drain the battery constantly; very high values make readings noisy unless a small capacitor is added at the ADC pin.

claim: A voltage divider scales a battery voltage down into an ADC's range: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
draft: Two resistors in series across the battery give a proportional, lower voltage at their midpoint that an ADC can read.

claim: A voltage divider scales a battery voltage down into an ADC's range: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
draft: Suppose a divider is sized for 7.4 V nominal; at 8.4 V full charge it overdrives the pin.

claim: A voltage divider scales a battery voltage down into an ADC's range: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
draft: Size it so a full pack reads below the ADC maximum with margin.

claim: A BSS138-based bidirectional level shifter safely connects 3.3 V and 5 V I2C devices.
draft: Links to the SCPBot Grove wiring and 3.3 V I/O cubes.

claim: A BSS138-based bidirectional level shifter safely connects 3.3 V and 5 V I2C devices.
draft: These shifters are slow, so they suit I2C and slow GPIO but not fast SPI.

claim: A BSS138-based bidirectional level shifter safely connects 3.3 V and 5 V I2C devices.
draft: A MOSFET-based shifter with pull-ups on both sides passes I2C signals in both directions between voltage domains.

claim: A BSS138-based bidirectional level shifter safely connects 3.3 V and 5 V I2C devices.
draft: Suppose a 5 V module is wired straight to the ESP32; its pull-ups put 5 V on 3.3 V pins.

claim: A BSS138-based bidirectional level shifter safely connects 3.3 V and 5 V I2C devices.
draft: Often unnecessary: powering a breakout at 3.3 V removes the need entirely.

claim: A bulk electrolytic capacitor across a servo power rail absorbs current spikes and reduces voltage dips.
draft: SCPBot: the PCA9685 breakout has a footprint for one on V+. Links to the MG90S stall-current cube.

claim: A bulk electrolytic capacitor across a servo power rail absorbs current spikes and reduces voltage dips.
draft: A capacitor covers milliseconds, not sustained draw; if the supply is too weak for the average load, no capacitor fixes it.

claim: A bulk electrolytic capacitor across a servo power rail absorbs current spikes and reduces voltage dips.
draft: A large electrolytic capacitor (commonly a few hundred to about 1000 µF) across V+ and GND supplies short bursts of current when servos start or stall, so the rail dips less.

claim: A bulk electrolytic capacitor across a servo power rail absorbs current spikes and reduces voltage dips.
draft: Suppose all eight servos start together; the capacitor fills the first spike and the UBEC catches up before the rail sags.

claim: A bulk electrolytic capacitor across a servo power rail absorbs current spikes and reduces voltage dips.
draft: Cheap insurance on any multi-servo build, but size the supply first.

claim: A capacitor's voltage rating should sit well above the highest voltage it will see.
draft: Never put a low-voltage cap where the raw 2S pack (8.4 V full) can reach it.

claim: A capacitor's voltage rating should sit well above the highest voltage it will see.
draft: Rule-of-thumb margins vary by source and capacitor type; the datasheet derating curve is the real guide.

claim: A capacitor's voltage rating should sit well above the highest voltage it will see.
draft: A common rule of thumb is to rate a capacitor at least 1.5 to 2 times the rail's maximum voltage.

claim: A capacitor's voltage rating should sit well above the highest voltage it will see.
draft: Suppose a 6.3 V cap sits on a rail that spikes to 7 V during regenerative braking; it ages fast and fails.

claim: A capacitor's voltage rating should sit well above the highest voltage it will see.
draft: On a 5–6 V servo rail, a 16 V capacitor is a sensible default.

claim: Large capacitors can hold charge after power is removed.
draft: Mains-voltage capacitors are a genuine shock hazard; hobby robot rails aren't.

claim: Large capacitors can hold charge after power is removed.
draft: At 5–8 V, the charge in hobby-size capacitors is a short-circuit risk, not a shock risk.

claim: Large capacitors can hold charge after power is removed.
draft: A large capacitor stays charged after disconnecting the supply until something discharges it.

claim: Large capacitors can hold charge after power is removed.
draft: Suppose the pack is unplugged and a wire is cut; the cap sparks across the cutters.

claim: Large capacitors can hold charge after power is removed.
draft: Short a probe across it, or wait, before reworking a board.

claim: Separately powered parts of a circuit must share a common ground for signals between them to work.
draft: SCPBot shares ground through the PCA9685. Links to the UBEC cubes.

claim: Separately powered parts of a circuit must share a common ground for signals between them to work.
draft: Heavy current returning through a shared signal ground can shift the reference; route high-current ground returns separately where possible.

claim: Separately powered parts of a circuit must share a common ground for signals between them to work.
draft: A signal is a voltage measured against ground; without a shared ground, the receiving device has no reference and reads garbage.

claim: Separately powered parts of a circuit must share a common ground for signals between them to work.
draft: Suppose the UBEC ground isn't joined to the M5's ground; PWM signals reach the servos with no reference, and they jitter.

claim: Separately powered parts of a circuit must share a common ground for signals between them to work.
draft: Star-ground the power returns, and keep the signal ground shared.

claim: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed close to an IC's power pins filters high-frequency noise.
draft: Distance matters: a long trace to the cap adds inductance and weakens it.

claim: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed close to an IC's power pins filters high-frequency noise.
draft: Most breakout boards already include one, so adding another usually changes little.

claim: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed close to an IC's power pins filters high-frequency noise.
draft: A 100 nF (0.1 µF) ceramic between VCC and GND, as close to the chip as possible, supplies fast current transients and shunts high-frequency noise.

claim: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed close to an IC's power pins filters high-frequency noise.
draft: Suppose a sensor resets randomly when servos move; a missing decoupling cap near it is a common cause.

claim: A 100 nF ceramic capacitor placed close to an IC's power pins filters high-frequency noise.
draft: Check the breakout first; add one when building on bare chips or perfboard.

claim: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can fail violently if fitted backwards.
draft: Tantalum capacitors are also polarised and fail short, sometimes with fire.

claim: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can fail violently if fitted backwards.
draft: Ceramic and most film capacitors aren't polarised, so the rule only applies to electrolytics and tantalums.

claim: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can fail violently if fitted backwards.
draft: An electrolytic capacitor has a marked negative lead (a stripe on the body, and usually the shorter leg); reversed, it can heat, vent or burst.

claim: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can fail violently if fitted backwards.
draft: Suppose a bulk cap goes in backwards on the servo rail; it bulges or pops at first power.

claim: Electrolytic capacitors are polarised and can fail violently if fitted backwards.
draft: Check the stripe before every power-up on a new board.

claim: A ferrite core on a switching regulator's leads reduces electrical noise.
draft: Many UBECs ship with a ferrite ring on the output lead.

claim: A ferrite core on a switching regulator's leads reduces electrical noise.
draft: A ferrite does little for low-frequency ripple; that's the bulk capacitor's job.

claim: A ferrite core on a switching regulator's leads reduces electrical noise.
draft: Switching regulators like UBECs produce high-frequency noise; a ferrite ring or bead on the leads damps it before it reaches sensitive parts.

claim: A ferrite core on a switching regulator's leads reduces electrical noise.
draft: Suppose the VL53L0X readings jitter only when servos move; switching noise on shared wiring is a likely cause.

claim: A ferrite core on a switching regulator's leads reduces electrical noise.
draft: Fit the one that came with the UBEC.

claim: A flyback diode across a DC motor or relay coil clamps the voltage spike when it's switched off.
draft: Relevant to Replicant's ESP32 TT-motor extension spec.

claim: A flyback diode across a DC motor or relay coil clamps the voltage spike when it's switched off.
draft: Hobby servos and most motor-driver modules already include protection, so this mainly matters when switching a bare motor or relay with a transistor.

claim: A flyback diode across a DC motor or relay coil clamps the voltage spike when it's switched off.
draft: Switching off an inductive load causes a voltage spike; a diode across the load, reverse-biased in normal operation, gives that energy a safe path.

claim: A flyback diode across a DC motor or relay coil clamps the voltage spike when it's switched off.
draft: Suppose a TT motor is switched by a bare MOSFET with no diode; the spike eventually kills the MOSFET.

claim: A flyback diode across a DC motor or relay coil clamps the voltage spike when it's switched off.
draft: Always add one when switching a coil directly from a MOSFET.

claim: A fuse protects the wiring, not the device downstream.
draft: Links to wire-gauge-sets-current.

claim: A fuse protects the wiring, not the device downstream.
draft: Polyfuses (PTC resettable fuses) are slower still and better for repeated minor faults than hard shorts.

claim: A fuse protects the wiring, not the device downstream.
draft: A fuse is sized to the wire it feeds, so the wire can't overheat; it reacts too slowly to save delicate electronics from a fault.

claim: A fuse protects the wiring, not the device downstream.
draft: Suppose a fuse is sized for a component's current; the thin wire to it burns first.

claim: A fuse protects the wiring, not the device downstream.
draft: Size the fuse from the wire gauge, then check it doesn't blow under normal peaks.

claim: An I2C bus needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL, typically between 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ.
draft: SCPBot shares one bus between the PCA9685 and VL53L0X. Links to the pca9685-boards-can-share-a-bus cube.

claim: An I2C bus needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL, typically between 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ.
draft: Each breakout often adds its own pull-ups, and several in parallel can pull too hard for the chips to drive low.

claim: An I2C bus needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL, typically between 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ.
draft: I2C lines are open-drain, so pull-up resistors to the logic voltage are what make them read high; values from about 2.2 kΩ to 10 kΩ are common.

claim: An I2C bus needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL, typically between 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ.
draft: Suppose a third breakout is added and the bus starts failing; stacked pull-ups are the first suspect.

claim: An I2C bus needs pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL, typically between 2.2 kΩ and 10 kΩ.
draft: Measure the combined pull-up before adding more boards.

claim: An inline fuse between the battery and the circuit turns a short circuit into a blown fuse instead of a fire.
draft: SCPBot: between the 2S packs and the UBEC.

claim: An inline fuse between the battery and the circuit turns a short circuit into a blown fuse instead of a fire.
draft: A fuse that's too small blows during normal servo stalls; too large and it protects nothing.

claim: An inline fuse between the battery and the circuit turns a short circuit into a blown fuse instead of a fire.
draft: A Li-ion pack can deliver far more current than any wire on a small robot can carry; a fuse near the pack's positive lead cuts it off on a fault.

claim: An inline fuse between the battery and the circuit turns a short circuit into a blown fuse instead of a fire.
draft: Suppose a screw pinches the power lead to the frame; with a fuse, it's a blown fuse, without one, a melted wire.

claim: An inline fuse between the battery and the circuit turns a short circuit into a blown fuse instead of a fire.
draft: Rate it above the normal peak draw and below what the wiring can carry.

claim: An LED needs a series resistor sized by R = (V supply − V forward) ÷ I.
draft: Example: 3.3 V, red LED at 2.0 V, 5 mA → (3.3 − 2.0) ÷ 0.005 = 260 Ω; use 270 Ω.

claim: An LED needs a series resistor sized by R = (V supply − V forward) ÷ I.
draft: Forward voltage varies by colour, roughly 1.8–2.2 V for red and 2.8–3.3 V for blue or white, so one resistor value doesn't fit every LED.

claim: An LED needs a series resistor sized by R = (V supply − V forward) ÷ I.
draft: Without a resistor an LED draws as much current as the source allows and burns out; R = (Vs − Vf) ÷ I sets the current.

claim: An LED needs a series resistor sized by R = (V supply − V forward) ÷ I.
draft: Suppose a white LED goes straight onto a 3.3 V pin; it may light, briefly, while stressing the GPIO.

claim: An LED needs a series resistor sized by R = (V supply − V forward) ÷ I.
draft: Aim for 5–10 mA for indicators on a 3.3 V GPIO; it's bright enough and easy on the pin.

claim: A logic-level N-channel MOSFET can switch a load from a 3.3 V GPIO if it's specified to switch fully on at that gate voltage.
draft: Common hobby examples include the AO3400 and IRLZ44N, but check each against your load.

claim: A logic-level N-channel MOSFET can switch a load from a 3.3 V GPIO if it's specified to switch fully on at that gate voltage.
draft: Gate threshold voltage, Vgs(th), is where it barely starts conducting, not where it's fully on; picking by threshold alone is a common mistake.

claim: A logic-level N-channel MOSFET can switch a load from a 3.3 V GPIO if it's specified to switch fully on at that gate voltage.
draft: MOSFETs are rated with Rds(on) at a specific gate voltage; for a 3.3 V GPIO, choose one rated at 2.5 V or 3.3 V Vgs, not one that only lists 10 V.

claim: A logic-level N-channel MOSFET can switch a load from a 3.3 V GPIO if it's specified to switch fully on at that gate voltage.
draft: Suppose a MOSFET with a 2 V threshold is driven at 3.3 V under load; it half-conducts and gets hot.

claim: A logic-level N-channel MOSFET can switch a load from a 3.3 V GPIO if it's specified to switch fully on at that gate voltage.
draft: Read Rds(on) at Vgs = 2.5 V or lower on the datasheet before buying.

claim: A MOSFET gate usually gets a small series resistor and a pull-down resistor to ground.
draft: Same boot-safety idea as holding PCA9685 OE high until init.

claim: A MOSFET gate usually gets a small series resistor and a pull-down resistor to ground.
draft: At low switching speeds the series resistor is optional; the pull-down is the one that matters.

claim: A MOSFET gate usually gets a small series resistor and a pull-down resistor to ground.
draft: A small series resistor (around 100 Ω) limits gate inrush current; a pull-down (around 10–100 kΩ) keeps the MOSFET off while the GPIO is floating at boot.

claim: A MOSFET gate usually gets a small series resistor and a pull-down resistor to ground.
draft: Suppose a motor MOSFET has no pull-down; the robot twitches every time the ESP32 resets.

claim: A MOSFET gate usually gets a small series resistor and a pull-down resistor to ground.
draft: Always fit the pull-down: an uncontrolled load at boot is a safety issue.

claim: Polarised connectors rated for the current prevent reversed connections and loose joints.
draft: Links to reverse-polarity-protection.

claim: Polarised connectors rated for the current prevent reversed connections and loose joints.
draft: Connector current ratings vary by manufacturer and clone quality; a cheap clone may not meet the original rating.

claim: Polarised connectors rated for the current prevent reversed connections and loose joints.
draft: Keyed connectors such as JST-XH (balance leads) and XT30 or XT60 (power) only fit one way round.

claim: Polarised connectors rated for the current prevent reversed connections and loose joints.
draft: Suppose the pack connects through Dupont jumpers; one slips off mid-walk, or gets plugged in reversed.

claim: Polarised connectors rated for the current prevent reversed connections and loose joints.
draft: Use XT30 or bigger for pack power, never Dupont jumpers.

claim: A pull-up or pull-down resistor stops an unconnected input from floating.
draft: Links to the M5StickC Plus2 3.3 V I/O cube.

claim: A pull-up or pull-down resistor stops an unconnected input from floating.
draft: The ESP32 has internal pull-ups and pull-downs on most pins, so an external resistor is often unnecessary. GPIO34–39 have none.

claim: A pull-up or pull-down resistor stops an unconnected input from floating.
draft: An input pin with nothing driving it picks up noise and reads random values; a resistor to VCC or GND gives it a defined default.

claim: A pull-up or pull-down resistor stops an unconnected input from floating.
draft: Suppose a button on GPIO35 has no resistor; the code registers presses that never happened.

claim: A pull-up or pull-down resistor stops an unconnected input from floating.
draft: Use the internal ones where available, external ones on input-only pins.

claim: A resistor must be rated for the power it dissipates, P = I² × R.
draft: Example: 2 A through 0.1 Ω = 0.4 W, so ¼ W isn't enough.

claim: A resistor must be rated for the power it dissipates, P = I² × R.
draft: Most signal resistors carry microamps or milliamps and never come close to their rating.

claim: A resistor must be rated for the power it dissipates, P = I² × R.
draft: Common through-hole resistors are rated ¼ W; dissipating more makes them overheat and drift or fail.

claim: A resistor must be rated for the power it dissipates, P = I² × R.
draft: Suppose a ¼ W resistor is used as a current sense on a 2 A servo rail; it dissipates far more than it can handle.

claim: A resistor must be rated for the power it dissipates, P = I² × R.
draft: Only check the rating where real current flows: shunts, LED strings, dummy loads.

claim: A series diode or a P-channel MOSFET protects a circuit if the battery is connected backwards.
draft: Polarised connectors (XT30, JST) prevent most reversals before protection is ever needed.

claim: A series diode or a P-channel MOSFET protects a circuit if the battery is connected backwards.
draft: A series diode wastes power at high current; on a several-amp servo rail it would get hot and drop the voltage noticeably.

claim: A series diode or a P-channel MOSFET protects a circuit if the battery is connected backwards.
draft: A diode in series blocks reverse current but drops voltage; a P-channel MOSFET wired for reverse protection does the same with far lower loss.

claim: A series diode or a P-channel MOSFET protects a circuit if the battery is connected backwards.
draft: Suppose the 2S pack is plugged in backwards with no protection; the UBEC may not survive.

claim: A series diode or a P-channel MOSFET protects a circuit if the battery is connected backwards.
draft: Use a diode on low-current logic supplies, a MOSFET on the servo rail.

claim: Schottky diodes drop less voltage than standard silicon diodes.
draft: Exact drop depends on current; check the datasheet curve.

claim: Schottky diodes drop less voltage than standard silicon diodes.
draft: Schottkys leak more current in reverse, especially when hot.

claim: Schottky diodes drop less voltage than standard silicon diodes.
draft: A Schottky diode typically drops around 0.2–0.45 V, versus about 0.6–0.7 V for a standard silicon diode.

claim: Schottky diodes drop less voltage than standard silicon diodes.
draft: Suppose a silicon diode drops 0.7 V from a 5 V rail; the servos run at 4.3 V, below their rating.

claim: Schottky diodes drop less voltage than standard silicon diodes.
draft: The usual choice for power paths and flyback on small motors.

claim: Wire gauge sets how much current a wire can safely carry.
draft: For a few amps of servo current, around 18–20 AWG is a common choice; check a table for your length.

claim: Wire gauge sets how much current a wire can safely carry.
draft: Published ampacity tables vary with insulation, length and bundling, so numbers differ by source.

claim: Wire gauge sets how much current a wire can safely carry.
draft: Thinner wire (higher AWG) has more resistance, heats more and drops more voltage at a given current.

claim: Wire gauge sets how much current a wire can safely carry.
draft: Suppose 26 AWG jumper wire feeds eight servos; it warms up and the rail sags at the servo end.

claim: Wire gauge sets how much current a wire can safely carry.
draft: Use thick, short wire for servo power and thin wire only for signals.
